# 1 Maccabees Chapter 9 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Verses:** 73 | **Disagreements:** 41

---

## Summary
This chapter narrates the death of Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan's assumption of leadership, and the guerrilla warfare period. Disagreements cluster around the emotional and theological language of the lament (vv.7, 10, 21), tactical military vocabulary, and the theological note on prophecy (v.27).

---

## Disagreements

**v.6** — "slipped away" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "deserted" (LOGOS) vs. "melted away" / "began slipping away" (PNEUMA)
- LOGOS chooses the stronger, more judgmental "deserted"; EMET and SOPHIA prefer the Greek's more neutral "slipped away"; PNEUMA splits: "began slipping away" in first clause, "slipping away" thereafter.

**v.7** — "crushed in spirit" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "crushed in spirit" (LOGOS) vs. "his heart broke within him" (PNEUMA)
- Agreement on "crushed" between EMET/LOGOS/SOPHIA; PNEUMA paraphrases with idiomatic English.

**v.8** — "gathered his strength" (LOGOS) vs. "was brought low and said" (EMET) vs. "summoned his courage" (PNEUMA) vs. "gathered himself" (SOPHIA)
- EMET preserves the literal Greek "was brought low"; LOGOS and PNEUMA interpret toward resolve; SOPHIA mediates.

**v.9** — "dissuaded him" (EMET) vs. "tried to turn him back" (LOGOS) vs. "urged him back" (PNEUMA/SOPHIA)
- Word choice divergence on the nature of the soldiers' response.

**v.10** — "Far be it from me" (all) — agreement; but "die bravely for our brothers" vs. "die like men" (PNEUMA)
- PNEUMA adds interpretive flourish ("like men"); others stay closer to the Greek.

**v.11** — "most powerful warriors" vs. "mighty men" (EMET) vs. "most powerful warriors" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "shock troops" (PNEUMA)
- PNEUMA uses modern military register; EMET stays archaic-biblical.

**v.12** — "phalanx" — agreement across all four translators; PNEUMA adds no gloss.

**v.13** — "the earth shook from the noise of the armies" — agreement; PNEUMA adds "colliding."

**v.15** — "Mount Azotus" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "slopes of Azotus" (PNEUMA) vs. "slope of Azotus" (SOPHIA)
- Minor geographic/descriptive divergence.

**v.17** — "fell wounded" (EMET) vs. "fell slain" / "fell wounded" divergence
- LOGOS says "fell slain" in v.40 context; here "fell wounded" — EMET consistent; minor.

**v.18** — "Then Judas fell" — agreement; PNEUMA adds no expansion here (restraint noted).

**v.21** — "How is the mighty one fallen" (EMET) vs. "How has the mighty fallen" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "How has the mighty warrior fallen" (PNEUMA)
- PNEUMA inserts "warrior" to clarify; others echo the biblical register more closely.
- "savior of Israel" (EMET/LOGOS/PNEUMA) vs. "Savior of Israel" (SOPHIA) — SOPHIA capitalizes for messianic resonance.

**v.22** — "acts" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "remaining acts" (LOGOS) vs. "full account" (PNEUMA)
- "The rest of the acts" formula: PNEUMA paraphrases; LOGOS/EMET/SOPHIA stay close to biblical formula.

**v.23** — "put out their heads" (EMET) vs. "raised their heads" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "crawled out of every corner" (PNEUMA)
- Idiomatic range from literal (EMET) to idiomatic (LOGOS) to vivid paraphrase (PNEUMA).

**v.24** — "a very great famine" (EMET) vs. "a very severe famine" (LOGOS) vs. "a terrible famine" (PNEUMA/SOPHIA)
- Greek: λιμὸς μέγας — translation of megas as "great/severe/terrible."

**v.25** — "deliberately chose" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) vs. "chose" (EMET)
- EMET omits the adverb; others add it to underscore the calculated evil.

**v.26** — "avenged himself on them" (EMET) vs. "took vengeance" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "made them suffer" (PNEUMA)
- Varying treatment of Greek ἐξεδίκησεν.

**v.27** — "a prophet ceased to appear to them" — agreement on theological note; PNEUMA paraphrases as "the last prophet had gone silent."
- The phrase signals the intertestamental period's silence; all translators preserve its gravity.

**v.28-30** — "ruler and leader" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "leader and commander" (LOGOS) vs. "commander and leader" (PNEUMA)
- Order and word choice of the leadership titles vary.

**v.33** — "pool of Asphar" — agreement; PNEUMA adds no gloss.

**v.34** — "he came, he and all his army, across the Jordan" (EMET) vs. "he came with all his forces across the Jordan" (LOGOS) — structural difference.

**v.35** — "leader of the company" (EMET) vs. "leader of the people" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "commander of the baggage train" (PNEUMA)
- PNEUMA significantly expands and clarifies the nature of John's role.

**v.37** — "daughter of one of the great nobles of Canaan" — agreement; PNEUMA clarifies "Canaan's most powerful nobles."

**v.38** — "remembered the blood of John their brother" — agreement; PNEUMA paraphrases "They thought of John their brother. And they moved." — dramatic compression.

**v.39** — "timbrels" (EMET) vs. "tambourines" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — instrument translation.

**v.40** — "killed them" (EMET) vs. "struck them down" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — variation in violence register.

**v.41** — "voice of their music into lamentation" — agreement; PNEUMA paraphrases "Music became weeping."

**v.44** — "it is not today as yesterday and the day before" (EMET) vs. "the situation today is not the same as before" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "today is not like yesterday or before" (PNEUMA)
- EMET preserves the Hebraistic idiom "yesterday and the day before."

**v.45** — "marsh and thicket" — agreement; PNEUMA adds "all around."

**v.46** — "cry to heaven" (EMET) vs. "cry out to Heaven" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — capitalization of Heaven diverges.

**v.48** — "leaped into the Jordan and swam across" — agreement; LOGOS says "jumped," PNEUMA says "dove."

**v.50** — "strongly fortified cities" (LOGOS) vs. "strong cities" (EMET) vs. "string of strongholds" (PNEUMA)

**v.53** — "leading men of the land" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "leading men of the land" (LOGOS) vs. "leading families of Judea" (PNEUMA)

**v.54** — "works of the prophets" (EMET) vs. "work of the prophets" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) — singular vs. plural.
- PNEUMA says "a structure that had been built by the prophets."

**v.55** — "mouth was stopped" (EMET) vs. "mouth was sealed" (SOPHIA) vs. "mouth was stopped" (LOGOS) vs. "mouth was locked shut" (PNEUMA)

**v.57** — "two years" — agreement.

**v.60** — "plot became known to them" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "the plot became known to Jonathan" (SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — named vs. anonymous.

**v.65** — "slipped away" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "left Simon his brother in the city and went out" (EMET) vs. "made a decision" then slipped out (PNEUMA) — narrative framing differs.

**v.66** — "began to strike and to go up with the forces" (EMET) — difficult Greek; LOGOS "they began to strike and advance into battle"; SOPHIA mediates; PNEUMA clarifies most.

**v.68** — "crushed by them" — agreement; PNEUMA adds "broke Bacchides."

**v.70** — "send ambassadors" (EMET) vs. "send envoys" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA)

**v.72** — "never to enter their borders again" (all) — agreement on this summary statement.

**v.73** — "exterminated the godless" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "destroyed the godless ones" (EMET) vs. "routing out every apostate" (PNEUMA)
- PNEUMA's "apostate" is an interpretive choice (implies Jews who abandoned the faith, not merely irreligious people).
